name: The Reasonable Person Standard
aliases: The man on the Clapham omnibus
statement: Conduct is judged not by what you thought was fine but by what an ordinarily prudent person would do.
statementAccent: what an ordinarily prudent person would do
meaning: The reasonable person standard is a legal test, central to negligence and tort law, that judges a person's conduct against how a hypothetical reasonable person, one of ordinary prudence and care, would have acted under the same or similar circumstances. It is an objective standard, measured by external community expectations rather than the particular defendant's own subjective beliefs. The reasonable person is a legal fiction, historically called the reasonable man and memorably personified in English law as the man on the Clapham omnibus, an ordinary member of the public. Developed in nineteenth-century common law, the standard sets the benchmark for the duty of care in negligence: a defendant is negligent if their conduct falls below what a reasonable person would do. It is a flexible, foundational tool throughout tort and criminal law.
mechanism: To decide whether conduct was careless, the law asks not what the defendant personally thought reasonable but what a reasonable person, an ordinarily prudent member of the community, would have done in the circumstances. Because the standard is objective, a defendant cannot escape liability by pointing to their own honest but mistaken judgement; they are held to the external benchmark. The reasonable person is imagined to consider risks, weigh alternatives, and exercise sensible judgement, so they are not merely the average person but an idealised prudent one. The standard adapts to context: children are judged by what a reasonable child of similar age, intelligence, and experience would do, and those undertaking skilled work are held to the higher standard of a reasonable professional, so the benchmark flexes while remaining objective.

examples.tag: The man on the Clapham omnibus
examples.text: English law personifies the reasonable person as the man on the Clapham omnibus, an ordinary member of the public against whom conduct is measured.
A defendant is negligent when their conduct falls below what a reasonable person would have done, the standard of care at the heart of tort law.
Children are judged by what a reasonable child of like age and experience would do, and professionals by the standard of a reasonable professional in the field.

variants.name: The professional standard
variants.text: The higher benchmark applied to those exercising a skill or profession, held to what a reasonable competent professional in that field would do.

variants.name: The child standard
variants.text: The adjusted standard for children, judged against a reasonable child of similar age, intelligence, and experience rather than an adult.

whyItMatters: The reasonable person standard is a foundational and remarkably flexible benchmark running through tort and criminal law, giving courts an objective yardstick for evaluating conduct without prying into the defendant's private thoughts. It defines the duty of care in negligence, shapes questions of reasonableness in self-defence and provocation, and anchors countless legal judgements about what care people owe one another. By measuring conduct against ordinary community expectations rather than individual belief, it promotes consistency and fairness while adapting to context through adjusted standards for children and professionals. Its blend of objectivity and flexibility has made the reasonable person one of the most enduring constructs in the common law.

working.text: judge conduct by what an ordinarily prudent person would have done in the circumstances, not by the defendant's own view.
hold defendants to the external community benchmark, so an honest but unreasonable belief is no defence to negligence.
apply the standard of a reasonable child for children and a reasonable professional for skilled work, flexing the benchmark while keeping it objective.

limits: Because the standard is objective, it does not fully account for a particular defendant's individual limitations, which some criticise as harsh; the law softens this only through defined adjustments, such as standards for children and professionals, and for some disabilities. The reasonable person is a construct, so applying it requires judgement about what such a person would do, which can vary among juries and judges. It sets the standard of conduct but does not by itself resolve causation or damages, and it can embed the assumptions of whoever imagines the reasonable person, raising concerns about whose norms the fictional figure reflects.
misreadings: The reasonable person is a hypothetical, idealised construct of ordinary prudence, not literally the average person and not the specific defendant, so it is not measured by what most people happen to do or by the defendant's own opinion. The standard asks what a reasonable person would do, an objective question, not what the defendant subjectively believed was reasonable, so honest but unreasonable conduct still falls short. And the benchmark is not rigidly uniform; it adjusts for children and for professionals, so it is objective without being one-size-fits-all.
origin: Developed in English and American common law in the nineteenth century, with the objective reasonable-person standard often traced to the 1837 English case Vaughan v Menlove, and personified in English law as the man on the Clapham omnibus.
